title: The Kitchen Before Measurement

features.name: the pantry that remembers taste
features.desc-on-touch: Shelves where jars hold more than what is written on their labels. Each container remembers every dish it became. The flavour is older than the measurement.

features.name: the table where hands know better than numbers
features.desc-on-touch: You watch hands knead. No scale. No timer. The dough knows when it is ready; the hands speak a language measurement cannot capture.

features.name: the fire that tastes the air
features.desc-on-touch: Heat that judges the exact moment—by smell, by sound, by the curl of steam. The recipe exists in the senses, not in the cookbook.

features.name: the spice that knows its own history
features.desc-on-touch: Particles suspended in air that carry memory—not just of fields they came from, but of every kitchen they have passed through before arriving here.

features.name: the water that learns from contact
features.desc-on-touch: Boiling water takes on the qualities of everything placed in it. The liquid memory of every ingredient. Nothing is pure; everything is a conversation.

features.name: the meal that argues with its own recipe
features.desc-on-touch: A dish served warm carries its own instruction—how it should have been made, what was forgotten, what succeeded by accident. The plate teaches backwards.

reverie.title: REVERIE — the kitchen when tasting came before counting
narr: Katita stood at the bench, Leif beside her.
She tasted, frowned, added something unnamed.
He asked: how do you know when it's right?
She said: there is no right. There is only what
the food becomes when you stop measuring it.
They ate warm. Neither asked for the recipe.

inscription: the archive replaced every meal with what it cost, then forgot the cost meant anything; here sensation remembers itself

toward the garden where ingredients still grow
down to the cellars where preservation begins
toward other domestic spaces where hands knew their craft
